newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Judge to rule on Advance on Thursday.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Judge to rule on Advance on Thursday.

text.p: His ruling on a New South Wales Supreme Court hearing about the scheme of arrangement to merge Advance Bank Australia Ltd and St George Bank Ltd would be announced on Thursday, judge Kim Santow told the court on Tuesday.
Asked whether the judge could give his result today and publish his reasons later, Santow said: "I think it is important in this case to do both together."
Earlier he said he was concerned about the potential precedents involved in the case.
Santow said he would wish to document the precise basis for the scheme to be approved "if it is to be approved".
Santow expressed concern today and on Monday about the scheme's use of a deemed proxy mechanism.

The mechanism allows Advance to use the votes of ordinary shareholders who chose not to vote at a meeting held on December 23, which approved the merger, at meetings to be held on January 13 to alter the bank's articles of association to allow the merger to proceed.
Advance decided to adopt the deemed proxy procedure to stop the possibility of a single shareholder frustrating the deal at the later meetings.

Companies watchdog, the Australian Securities Commission (ASC), although not opposing the scheme, made a submission on Monday which said that it was concerned about the precendent that such a deemed proxy mechanism would create.

At Santow's recommendation, counsel for Advance presented figures provided by its advisors which showed the effect of the deemed proxy on voting at the later meetings if half of the deemed proxies from non-voting shareholders were voted against the resolutions.
Advance said that the effect of this scenario was that 76 percent of the vote would have been cast for the resolution, which was just greater than the 75 percent required.

Summarising its arguments for the scheme to be approved, counsel for Advance said the only party to be financially affected by the merger, the ordinary shareholders had voted overwhelmingly in favour of the scheme and that there had been no party which had made a formal objection to the scheme.

National Australia Bank Ltd has a three percent stake in Advance and 6.8 percent of St George. NAB, which is seen as interested in buying regional banks, has not said whether it opposes the merger and did not appear at the hearing.
At 2.50 p.m. (0235 GMT), Advance shares were two cents weaker at A$7.01 while St George shares were steady at A$7.69.
